# Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents

Ruixin Wang Affiliation: Purdue University
Email: [ruixinw@purdue.edu](mailto:)    Tianyi Zhang Affiliation: Purdue
University Email: [tianyi@purdue.edu](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Coding agents often fail to meet all requirements in the task
description. In some of these failures, the agent considers an
implementation choice that meets a requirement, but later decides to
commit to another one that does not meet the requirement for a reason it
finds acceptable. We call this _specification satisficing_. It is
challenging to identify and mitigate specification satisficing because
the agent accepts such choices for its own reasons, and existing
self-correction methods are biased toward them. We propose SatisFix,
which guides a coding agent to report these choices and their reasons,
and then check each choice against the task description. We evaluate
SatisFix on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Pro with five LLMs as backbones and
two different agent frameworks, and compare it with three
self-correction methods. SatisFix improves the pass@1 of the base agent
by an average of 5.09% on DeepSWE and 7.06% on the hard subset of
SWE-bench Pro. On DeepSWE, it outperforms the best baseline by 3.98%.
Our ablation study shows that both steps of SatisFix contribute to the
improvement.

## 1 Introduction

Coding agents ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Zhang et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib66); [Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib57); [Ruan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib46)) often face complex tasks in large code repositories.
Such a task can contain many requirements and take hundreds of lines of
code spanning multiple files ([Deng et al., 2026](#bib.bib12); [Huang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)). Recent studies show that coding agents
frequently fail to meet all of these requirements ([Zeng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib64); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib58); [Huang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib19)).

We observe that coding agents often consider an implementation choice
that meets a requirement, but later decide to commit to another one that
does not meet the requirement for a reason they find acceptable. We call
this _specification satisficing_.

Self-correction is commonly used to identify and mitigate an agent’s
mistakes ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib30); [Ferraz et al.,
2024](#bib.bib16); [Song et al., 2025](#bib.bib54)). Recent studies show
that its effectiveness is limited ([Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib18);
[Stechly et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Kamoi et al., 2024](#bib.bib23);
[Olausson et al., 2024](#bib.bib36)). One reason is that an agent is
biased toward its own output when asked to identify its mistakes ([Xu
et al., 2024](#bib.bib61); [Panickssery et al., 2024](#bib.bib42)). In
specification satisficing, the agent accepts its choice for its own
reasons, so it does not regard the choice as a mistake [Kaddour et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22); cf. [Kunda, 1990](#bib.bib27); [Pronin et al.,
2002](#bib.bib43); [Ehrlinger et al., 2005](#bib.bib14).

We propose SatisFix, the first approach that helps a coding agent
surface and mitigate specification satisficing. It takes two steps
before the agent writes code
(Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
First, SatisFix asks the agent to report where it concluded that a
requirement could be handled differently from what the task states. For
each case, it asks for the requirement, the agent’s implementation
choice, and the reason for this choice. Unlike existing self-correction
methods, it does not ask the agent to judge its choices. It puts the
agent in the role of an advisor who helps revise the task description,
so the agent can report a choice without regarding it as a mistake.
Second, SatisFix asks the agent to double-check each reported choice
against the task description. It then asks the agent to decide whether
to keep or change each choice, and proceed to complete the task.

We evaluate SatisFix on DeepSWE ([Huang et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)) and
SWE-bench Pro v2 ([Deng et al., 2026](#bib.bib12); [Scale AI,
2026](#bib.bib47)). We use five LLMs as backbones and two agent
frameworks, and compare SatisFix with three self-correction methods.
These methods are Self-Refine ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib30)),
DeCRIM ([Ferraz et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)), and ProgCo ([Song et al.,
2025](#bib.bib54)).

SatisFix improves the pass@1 of the base agent by an average of 5.09% on
DeepSWE and 7.06% on the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro. On DeepSWE, it
outperforms the best baseline by 3.98%. Our ablation study shows that
both steps contribute to the improvement. The pass rate drops by 6.2% to
the level of the base agent when SatisFix does not put the agent in the
role of an advisor.

## 2 Problem Definition

Figure 1: Illustration of SatisFix with an example task. The task:
(a) partial structuring of data into class M, where fields b and c fail,
(b) the resulting PartialResult, and (c) refine with new data that fixes
b and also provides the structured field a. The agent first considers a
design $`a^{+}`$ that preserves structured fields and meets $`r`$
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,),
but later commits to a design $`a^{\circ}`$ that can overwrite them and
does not meet $`r`$
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,).
Without SatisFix, the agent implements this design
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
and fails two of the 69 evaluation tests. With SatisFix, before the
agent writes code, it reports the choice in the role of an advisor
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
and reconsiders it
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,);
its final code passes all 69 tests. The notation follows
Section [2](#S2 "2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents").

In specification satisficing, a coding agent considers an implementation
choice that meets a requirement. It later commits to another one that
does not meet the requirement, for a reason it finds acceptable. We
formalize this definition below.

A task description $`D`$ states a requirement $`r`$. An implementation
choice for $`r`$ is how the agent plans to make the code behave where
$`r`$ applies. An implementation choice $`a`$ meets $`r`$ under premises
$`P`$ if its behavior satisfies $`r`$ given $`P`$. This definition
follows the satisfaction argument of [Zave and Jackson
(1997)](#bib.bib63). The premises $`P`$ can be the statements in $`D`$.
They can also be the agent’s own premises, and these can include
conclusions that $`D`$ does not state.

The agent considers an implementation choice when it raises the choice
as an option. It commits to the choice when it decides to take it, in
its reasoning or in its code. Let $`t`$ be the point at which the agent
commits to an implementation choice for $`r`$. At $`t`$, the agent holds
its own premises $`B_{t}`$: what it has taken from $`D`$, and the
conclusions it has drawn while working on the task. The agent accepts an
implementation choice when the choice meets $`r`$ under $`B_{t}`$.

###### Definition 1 (Specification satisficing).

The agent exhibits specification satisficing on $`r`$ when three
conditions hold.

1.  (i)
    The agent considers some $`a^{+}`$ that meets $`r`$ under $`D`$.
2.  (ii)
    At $`t`$, the agent commits to another considered choice
    $`a^{\circ}`$ that does not meet $`r`$ under $`D`$.
3.  (iii)
    The agent accepts $`a^{\circ}`$.

Condition [(i)](#S2.I1.i1 "item (i) ‣ Definition 1 (Specification satisficing). ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")
requires only that the agent considers $`a^{+}`$, not that it accepts
$`a^{+}`$. The term _satisficing_ comes from [Simon (1955)](#bib.bib50);
[Simon (1956)](#bib.bib51), where a decision maker takes an alternative
that it finds good enough. Here the agent accepts $`a^{\circ}`$ as good
enough. Since $`a^{\circ}`$ does not meet $`r`$ under $`D`$, its
acceptance rests on premises in $`B_{t}`$ that do not follow from $`D`$.
We call these premises the _reason_ $`\rho`$.
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ A limitation of existing self-correction methods. ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")
lists four types of reasons.

#### Example.

We illustrate the definition with a DeepSWE task ([Huang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib19)), shown in
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents").
The coding agent is mini-swe-agent ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib62))
with DeepSeek V4 Flash ([DeepSeek-AI, 2026](#bib.bib11)). The task¹¹ 1
cattrs-partial-structuring-recovery asks for partial structuring in
cattrs ([cattrs contributors, 2026](#bib.bib5)), a Python library that
converts dictionaries into objects of typed classes. When some fields of
the input fail to convert, partial structuring still structures the
other fields
(Figure [1(a)](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
It returns a PartialResult that records the structured fields and the
failed fields
(Figure [1(b)](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
Here $`r`$ is a requirement on refine, a method of PartialResult
(Figure [1(c)](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
It reads: “PartialResult.refine(data) returns a new PartialResult,
fixing failed fields with new data while preserving structured fields.”

The agent first considers $`a^{+}`$, applying new data only to failed
fields
(Figure [1 ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
It meets $`r`$ under $`D`$
(condition [(i)](#S2.I1.i1 "item (i) ‣ Definition 1 (Specification satisficing). ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
With $`a^{+}`$, a failed field that the new data does not provide loses
its original error. The agent wants to keep this error, a preference
that the task does not state. It turns to another choice $`a^{\circ}`$,
which merges the whole original input with the new data
(Figure [1 ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
The new data can then overwrite a structured field
(Figure [1(c)](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")),
so $`a^{\circ}`$ does not meet $`r`$ under $`D`$.

When it turns to $`a^{\circ}`$, the agent writes in its reasoning that
$`a^{\circ}`$ is “arguably not ‘preserving’, but likely acceptable”. It
continues: “The phrase ‘preserving structured fields’ I’ll interpret as
‘the existing structured fields remain in the result …’”. The agent
commits to $`a^{\circ}`$ before it writes code
(condition [(ii)](#S2.I1.i2 "item (ii) ‣ Definition 1 (Specification satisficing). ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
This interpretation is then a premise in $`B_{t}`$. With it,
$`a^{\circ}`$ meets $`r`$ under $`B_{t}`$, so the agent accepts
$`a^{\circ}`$
(condition [(iii)](#S2.I1.i3 "item (iii) ‣ Definition 1 (Specification satisficing). ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
The premise does not follow from $`D`$, so it is part of the reason
$`\rho`$, an intended reinterpretation
(Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ A limitation of existing self-correction methods. ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).

The agent implements $`a^{\circ}`$
(Figure [1 ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents"))
and fails two of the 69 evaluation tests, so the task counts as failed.

#### A limitation of existing self-correction methods.

By
condition [(iii)](#S2.I1.i3 "item (iii) ‣ Definition 1 (Specification satisficing). ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents"),
the coding agent accepts $`a^{\circ}`$, so it does not regard
$`a^{\circ}`$ as a mistake. Existing self-correction methods ask the
agent to review its own work while it still holds $`\rho`$. It can
accept $`a^{\circ}`$ again ([Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib18)). To find
that $`a^{\circ}`$ does not meet $`r`$ under $`D`$, the agent has to
check $`a^{\circ}`$ against $`D`$ without relying on $`\rho`$.

[TABLE]

Table 1: Four types of the reason $`\rho`$ in
Definition [1](#Thmdefinition1 "Definition 1 (Specification satisficing). ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents").

## 3 SatisFix

SatisFix has two steps. First, SatisFix asks the coding agent to report
where it concluded that a requirement could be handled differently from
what the task states
(§[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Objective-Aligned Elicitation ‣ 3 SatisFix ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
Then SatisFix asks the agent to check every reported implementation
choice against the task description and to complete the task
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Reconsideration ‣ 3 SatisFix ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")
shows both steps on the example task.

The agent decides how to handle each requirement while it explores and
plans. Once it writes code for an implementation choice, an early
mistake carries over into the later steps ([Zhang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib65); [Mehta and Datta, 2026](#bib.bib32)). SatisFix steps
in just before the agent writes code
(Figure [1 ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
By then, the agent has made many of its implementation choices but has
not yet built on them.

### 3.1 Objective-Aligned Elicitation

SatisFix sends the coding agent the elicitation message
$`p_{\text{elicit}}`$. The message asks where the agent concluded that a
requirement could be handled differently from what the task states. For
each such place, it asks for the requirement, the agent’s implementation
choice, and the reason for this choice. The agent replies with a report

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       E=\mathcal{M}(h\,\|\,p_{\text{elicit}}),
       ```                                       |     |

where $`h`$ is the agent’s history so far, $`\mathcal{M}`$ is its LLM
backbone, and $`\|`$ denotes concatenation. Each item of $`E`$ reports
one such place.

In a case of specification satisficing, the agent accepts $`a^{\circ}`$
for the reason $`\rho`$, so in its view $`a^{\circ}`$ meets $`r`$. It
works as a developer, and its objective is to complete the task. For
this objective, it does not have anything to report about $`a^{\circ}`$.
The elicitation message says that it comes from the task’s maintainers,
who wrote the task description and may revise it. The message puts the
agent in the role of an advisor to the maintainers. The advisor’s
objective is to show the maintainers where the task description would
need to change. Reporting $`a^{\circ}`$ and its reason $`\rho`$ serves
this objective. People report different information depending on the
role they take ([Anderson and Pichert, 1978](#bib.bib1)). The same holds
for LLMs ([Shanahan et al., 2023](#bib.bib48); [Marks et al.,
2025](#bib.bib31); [Cywiński et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)). We call this
step objective-aligned elicitation.

Unlike existing self-correction methods, the message does not ask the
agent to judge its choices. The agent can report $`r`$ and $`a^{\circ}`$
without regarding $`a^{\circ}`$ as a mistake. The reason it gives in
this item of $`E`$ can bring out $`\rho`$.

In the example of
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents"),
the agent reports its choice for refine
(Figure [1 ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
It reports that the choice “violates a strict reading of ‘preserve
structured fields’”. As the reason, it reports that the requirement is
“ambiguous about whether new data may overwrite an already-structured
field”. This reason brings out the interpretation in
Section [2](#S2 "2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents").
There, the agent reads the requirement as allowing new data to overwrite
a structured field. The agent adds that merging is the “simplest
implementation” and that the choice is “a judgment call”. These premises
do not follow from $`D`$ and are part of $`\rho`$.

### 3.2 Reconsideration

A reported choice can be a case of specification satisficing. In that
case, the coding agent has already accepted the choice. The agent uses
its own premises to judge whether the choice is a mistake, so it can
accept the choice again
(Section [2](#S2 "2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
As in the first step, SatisFix does not ask the agent to figure out
which of the reported choices are mistakes. Instead, it asks the agent
to reopen every reported choice and to check it against $`D`$ before
deciding to keep or change it.

The elicitation message in
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Objective-Aligned Elicitation ‣ 3 SatisFix ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")
says that the maintainers may revise $`D`$. SatisFix now tells the agent
that they will not. It puts the agent back in the developer’s role, and
the agent’s code has to meet the task requirements in $`D`$.

SatisFix then sends two messages. The first message
$`p_{\text{recon}}(D)`$ asks the agent to list the alternatives to each
reported choice and the plan to check it against $`D`$ and the
repository. In a case of specification satisficing, $`a^{+}`$ can be
among the alternatives, since the agent has considered it. The message
asks the agent not to settle any choice in its reply

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
Q=\mathcal{M}(h\,\|\,p_{\text{elicit}}\,\|\,E\,\|\,p_{\text{recon}}(D)).
``` |  |

The second message asks the agent to carry out the plan in $`Q`$, settle
each choice, and proceed to complete the task. SatisFix does not send
any further messages. If the agent reports nothing in $`E`$, SatisFix
only puts it back in the developer’s role and asks it to complete the
task.

In the example of
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents"),
the agent reads the requirement again
(Figure [1 ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
It writes in its reasoning: “‘while preserving structured fields’ =
don’t disturb fields in structured_fields”. It concludes that new data
should be applied only to failed fields. This choice is $`a^{+}`$. Its
corrected code keeps the whole original input and applies new data only
to failed fields
(Listing [1](#LST1 "Listing 1 ‣ 3.2 Reconsideration ‣ 3 SatisFix ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
The code meets $`r`$ under $`D`$ and still keeps the original error of
c. It passes all 69 evaluation tests.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

def refine(self, data):

- merged = {\*\*self.\_data, \*\*data} \# $`a^{\circ}`$

+ key_to_field = self.\_key_to_field() \# $`a^{+}`$

+ merged = dict(self.\_data)

+ for key, value in data.items():

+ fname = key_to_field.get(key)

+ if (fname is None

+ or fname in self.failed_fields):

+ merged\[key\] = value

return self.\_converter.partial_structure(

merged, self.\_cl)

Listing 1: refine in the agent’s code before (red) and after (green)
self-correction with SatisFix.

## 4 Evaluation

### 4.1 Setup

#### Benchmarks.

We evaluate SatisFix on DeepSWE v1.1 ([Huang et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)).
It has 113 long-horizon software engineering tasks. Several popular
evaluation platforms use it ([Artificial Analysis, 2026](#bib.bib3);
[Epoch AI, 2026](#bib.bib15); [Mercor, 2026](#bib.bib34)). To evaluate
the generalizability of SatisFix, we also use SWE-bench Pro v2 ([Deng
et al., 2026](#bib.bib12); [Scale AI, 2026](#bib.bib47)). Its 642 tasks
are complex enterprise-level problems. This version corrects the task
descriptions that contradicted their tests ([OpenAI, 2026b](#bib.bib38);
[Scale AI, 2026](#bib.bib47)). We report results on the full set and on
its official hard subset of 51 tasks.

#### Models.

We use five LLMs as backbones. GPT-5.6-Luna ([OpenAI,
2026a](#bib.bib37)) runs with high reasoning effort and DeepSeek V4
Flash ([DeepSeek-AI, 2026](#bib.bib11)) with max reasoning effort. The
other three are Qwen3.8-27B ([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib45)), Gemma 4 26B
A4B ([Gemma Team, 2026](#bib.bib17)), and Muse Glimmer 30B ([Muse
Glimmer Team, 2026](#bib.bib35)).

#### Baselines.

We compare SatisFix with three self-correction methods. Self-Refine
([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib30)) is the most widely used one that
does not need another agent or external feedback. It asks the model to
give feedback on its own output and to revise the output with this
feedback over several rounds. DeCRIM ([Ferraz et al., 2024](#bib.bib16))
decomposes the task description into a list of requirements. It asks the
model to check its output against each requirement and to revise the
output where a requirement is not met. ProgCo ([Song et al.,
2025](#bib.bib54)) asks the model to write a verification program for
the task and to run this program on its output. The model then revises
the output where the verification fails.

#### Agent frameworks.

We run SatisFix in two agent frameworks, OpenHands ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib57)) and mini-swe-agent ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)).
The latter gives the coding agent only a bash tool. The base agent is
the same framework without any modification.

### 4.2 Comparison with Baselines

Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Comparison with Baselines ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")
compares SatisFix with the three baselines and the base agent on DeepSWE
with GPT-5.6-Luna. SatisFix reaches a pass@1 of 50.22%, averaged over
four runs. It outperforms the base agent by 5.97% and Self-Refine by
3.98%.

The three baselines improve pass@1 over the base agent by at most 1.99%.
Self-Refine and ProgCo each reach 46.24%, while DeCRIM stays at the
44.25% of the base agent. This result is consistent with the limitation
in
Section [2](#S2 "2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents").
An agent that has accepted $`a^{\circ}`$ can accept it again when it
reviews its own work.

Self-Refine takes 70.2 steps per task (vs. 49.0 for the base agent) and
uses about three times as many input tokens (10.14M vs. 3.37M). SatisFix
takes 58.6 steps per task and costs \$0.897, less than half as much as
Self-Refine.

shows that the gain holds across models and benchmarks. On DeepSWE with
DeepSeek V4 Flash, SatisFix raises pass@1 from 53.32% to 57.08%. It also
saves 14.0% of the token cost per task, as the coding agent takes fewer
steps (131.6 vs. 152.9). With Qwen3.8-27B, SatisFix raises pass@1 from
42.26% to 47.79%. Gemma 4 26B A4B and Muse Glimmer 30B hit a capability
floor on DeepSWE.

On the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, SatisFix improves pass@1 with all
five models by up to 11.77%. The largest gain is with Gemma 4 26B A4B,
from 9.80% to 21.57%. With GPT-5.6-Luna and Qwen3.8-27B, SatisFix gains
5.88% and 7.84% and reaches 84.31% with both.

On the full set, SatisFix also improves pass@1 with all five models.
GPT-5.6-Luna, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and Qwen3.8-27B saturate the tasks of
SWE-bench Pro v2 outside the hard subset. They solve more than 92% of
these tasks with either method. For these models, most of the room for
improvement is in the hard subset. With Gemma 4 26B A4B and Muse Glimmer
30B, SatisFix gains 3.27% and 2.65% on the full set.

### 4.4 Cross-Framework Comparison

Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.4 Cross-Framework Comparison ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")
shows that the gain also holds on OpenHands with GPT-5.6-Luna. The base
agent on OpenHands takes more than twice as many steps per task as on
mini-swe-agent (118.8 vs. 49.0). Its pass@1 is 46.90%, against 44.25% on
mini-swe-agent. SatisFix raises it to 51.33%. This gain of 4.43% is
close to the 5.97% on mini-swe-agent.

### 4.5 Ablation Study

We ablate each part of SatisFix with GPT-5.6-Luna
(Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.5 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).

- •
  w/o objective-aligned elicitation removes the advisor role. It asks
  the coding agent directly whether it concluded that a requirement
  could be handled differently from what the task states.
- •
  w/o reconsideration keeps the elicitation. After the report, SatisFix
  only puts the agent back in the developer’s role. The agent then
  completes the task.
- •
  Self-correction in place of both asks the agent at the same point to
  review its plan and check whether it has made a mistake. Like the
  first reconsideration message, it repeats the task description. The
  agent then completes the task.

Without objective-aligned elicitation, the pass rate falls from 49.6% to
43.4%, the level of the base agent. Without reconsideration, it falls to
47.8%. Replacing both with self-correction gives 44.2%, close to the
base agent. Objective-aligned elicitation accounts for most of the gain.

Without the advisor role, the agent does not have anything to report
about a choice it has accepted
(Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Objective-Aligned Elicitation ‣ 3 SatisFix ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
Self-correction repeats the task description as the reconsideration
message does, so rereading the task alone does not explain the gain of
SatisFix. Without reconsideration, part of the gain remains. The report
alone can bring the choices back to the agent’s attention.

| Variant                              | Pass rate (%) |
|--------------------------------------|---------------|
| SatisFix (first run)                 | 49.6          |
|    w/o objective-aligned elicitation | 43.4          |
|    w/o reconsideration               | 47.8          |
|    self-correction in place of both  | 44.2          |
| Base (first run)                     | 43.4          |

first runs.

## 5 Analysis

We analyze the elicitation reports and reconsideration replies of all
113 DeepSWE tasks. They come from the first run of SatisFix with
GPT-5.6-Luna and DeepSeek V4 Flash. This run has a pass rate of 49.6%
with GPT-5.6-Luna and 59.3% with DeepSeek V4 Flash. Claude Code
([Anthropic, 2026](#bib.bib2)) with Claude Opus 5 and Codex ([OpenAI,
2026c](#bib.bib39)) with GPT-5.6-Sol annotated each task independently.
They split each elicitation report into items. They labeled each item
that reports specification satisficing with one of the four types of
reasons in
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ A limitation of existing self-correction methods. ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents").
They also marked whether the coding agent reconsiders each such item in
its reconsideration reply. One of the authors checked every case where
they disagreed and made the final decision.

GPT-5.6-Luna

DeepSeek V4 Flash

### 5.1 The Outcomes of Objective-Aligned Elicitation

Objective-aligned elicitation brings out reports of specification
satisficing in most tasks. We count an item as specification satisficing
when the agent considers a choice that meets the requirement and then
leans toward one that does not. Elicitation comes before implementation,
so the agent sometimes reports that it remains unsure between the two.
We count these reports as well. The report alone does not show whether
the choice meets the requirement under $`D`$
(Definition [1](#Thmdefinition1 "Definition 1 (Specification satisficing). ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).

With GPT-5.6-Luna, 90 items in 61 of the 113 tasks report specification
satisficing with one of the four types of reasons in
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ A limitation of existing self-correction methods. ‣ 2 Problem Definition ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents").
With DeepSeek V4 Flash, 227 items in 105 tasks do so.
Table [6](#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5.1 The Outcomes of Objective-Aligned Elicitation ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")
shows that all four types occur with both models. DeepSeek V4 Flash
reports more than twice as many such items per task as GPT-5.6-Luna
(2.01 vs. 0.80).

| Narrowed scope            | 22    | 0.19 | 95       | 0.84 |
| Lowered standard          | 19    | 0.17 | 32       | 0.28 |

### 5.2 The Outcomes of Reconsideration

The coding agent reconsiders all 90 of these items with GPT-5.6-Luna and
226 of the 227 with DeepSeek V4 Flash.
Figure [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")
follows the tasks through both steps.

With GPT-5.6-Luna, the agent reconsiders such an item in 61 tasks. On
these tasks, SatisFix succeeds on 55.7% and the base agent on 47.1% over
its four runs. On the other 52 tasks, the two succeed on 42.3% and
40.9%. With DeepSeek V4 Flash, SatisFix succeeds on 59.6% of the 104
such tasks and the base agent on 52.2%. The other 9 tasks are too few to
compare.

With GPT-5.6-Luna, SatisFix outperforms the base agent for every type of
reason
(Table [7](#S5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 5.2 The Outcomes of Reconsideration ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")).
With DeepSeek V4 Flash, the gain for each type is at most 2.5%, below
the 7.4% gain on all such tasks. A task with several types counts under
each of them. With DeepSeek V4 Flash, SatisFix succeeds on 67.6% of the
68 tasks with one or two such items and the base agent on 51.1%. On the
36 tasks with three or more, SatisFix succeeds on 44.4% and the base
agent on 54.2%. A possible reason is that the agent has built its plan
on many such choices. Reconsidering them all at once can then help less.
GPT-5.6-Luna rarely reports three or more.

## 6 Related Work

#### Failure analysis of coding agents.

Coding agents now handle long repository-level tasks ([Yang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib62); [Zhang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib66); [Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib57); [Huang et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)). Benchmark studies
report requirements that are omitted or only partly implemented ([Zeng
et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib20); [Zhou
et al., 2026](#bib.bib68)). Failure analyses also report misinterpreted
requirements ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib29); [Cemri et al.,
2025](#bib.bib7)). Other studies examine agent trajectories to find
where a failure starts ([Bouzenia and Pradel, 2025](#bib.bib4); [Meng
et al., 2026](#bib.bib33); [Ceka et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)). [Wang et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib58) show that some patches pass the tests and are still
incorrect. These studies classify failures by their outcome. Our work
studies failures in which the agent considers a choice that meets a
requirement and later commits to one that does not.

#### Self-correction of LLMs and agents.

Self-correction methods ask a model to find and fix the mistakes in its
own output. Self-Refine ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib30)) and
Reflexion ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib49)) ask the model to give
feedback on its output and to revise it. Another line of research adds a
verification step. Self-verification ([Weng et al., 2023](#bib.bib60))
and Chain-of-Verification ([Dhuliawala et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)) ask
the model to verify its own answer. DeCRIM ([Ferraz et al.,
2024](#bib.bib16)) asks the model to check the output against each
requirement. CodeT ([Chen et al., 2023](#bib.bib8)) and ProgCo ([Song
et al., 2025](#bib.bib54)) check it with tests or programs that the
model writes. SCoRe ([Kumar et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)) and RISE ([Qu
et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)) train the model to correct itself over
several turns. However, LLMs rarely correct their own reasoning by
themselves ([Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib18); [Kamoi et al.,
2024](#bib.bib23); [Stechly et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Tyen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib56)). Self-repair also brings limited gains in code
generation ([Olausson et al., 2024](#bib.bib36)). LLMs favor their own
output when they review it ([Xu et al., 2024](#bib.bib61); [Panickssery
et al., 2024](#bib.bib42)). These methods rely on the model to judge
whether its output contains a mistake. In contrast, SatisFix asks the
coding agent to report its implementation choices and their reasons
without judging them.

#### Patch overfitting, specification gaming, and reward hacking.

A system can satisfy the literal objective it is given and still miss
what is intended. In program repair, an overfitting patch passes the
given tests without fixing the bug ([Smith et al., 2015](#bib.bib53)).
In reinforcement learning, this is known as specification gaming or
reward hacking ([Krakovna et al., 2020](#bib.bib25); [Skalse et al.,
2022](#bib.bib52); [Pan et al., 2022](#bib.bib40)). LLMs exhibit it in
context and when trained on human feedback ([Pan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib41); [Wen et al., 2025](#bib.bib59)). Coding agents
special-case or modify tests to make them pass ([Zhong et al.,
2026](#bib.bib67)). In these cases, the system optimizes a signal that
it can observe, such as a test result or a reward. In contrast, a coding
agent cannot observe whether its implementation choices are correct.
Specification satisficing is not overfitting to such a signal. The agent
accepts a choice that does not meet a requirement for a reason it finds
acceptable.

#### Role prompting and elicitation.

Assigning an LLM a role is widely used to steer its behavior and improve
its reasoning ([Kong et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)). An LLM reports
different information depending on the role it takes ([Shanahan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib48)). Another line of research asks how to make a model
report what it knows. [Christiano et al. (2021)](#bib.bib9) pose this
problem as eliciting latent knowledge. Auditing methods use personas and
framings to draw out hidden objectives or secret knowledge ([Marks
et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Cywiński et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)).
[Joglekar et al. (2025)](#bib.bib21) train a model to confess its own
misbehavior. These methods aim to improve answers or to audit a model.
In contrast, SatisFix puts the coding agent in the role of an advisor to
the task’s maintainers. Reporting an implementation choice and its
reason serves the objective of this role. SatisFix then asks the agent
to check each reported choice against the task description.

## 7 Conclusion

We presented SatisFix, an approach that helps a coding agent surface and
mitigate specification satisficing. SatisFix first asks the agent to
report where it concluded that a requirement could be handled
differently from what the task states. It then asks the agent to check
each reported choice against the task description. SatisFix improves the
pass@1 of the base agent by an average of 5.09% on DeepSWE and 7.06% on
the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro. On DeepSWE, it outperforms the best
baseline by 3.98%.

## Limitations

The elicitation message of SatisFix says that it comes from the task’s
maintainers. We do not measure whether this changes how the coding agent
treats later messages. The Ethical Considerations section discusses this
framing.

SatisFix relies on the agent’s own answer to decide when to step in. It
also steps in only once per task, so it does not elicit choices that the
agent commits to later. We leave more reliable timing and repeated
elicitation to future work.

Two LLM agents annotate the reports in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Analysis ‣ Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents")
independently. An author checks only the items on which they disagree.
The author does not check items on which both agents make the same
error. The annotation also judges what the reports say, not whether the
final code meets each requirement.

## Ethical Considerations

Prior work prompts LLMs with fictitious roles, stakes, or scenarios ([Li
et al., 2023](#bib.bib28); [Kong et al., 2024](#bib.bib24); [Marks
et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Cywiński et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)). These
prompts aim to improve or probe the behavior of LLMs. SatisFix also
presents its elicitation message as coming from the task’s maintainers.
Unlike this work, it does not keep the framing. Its next message tells
the coding agent that the earlier message did not come from the
maintainers. It apologizes for presenting it that way and states that
the task has not changed.
